title: Ananda and Rahula (Kern ch. 9)
hook: the attendant and the son receive their promises too

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man lived poor for years with a priceless jewel sewn into his coat, until a friend said look. Your line: the jewel in the coat. What did you find in your own lining? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

Keep watching a film after the stars' names roll by. Far down the credits, in small type, there's the person who held the umbrella between takes, the one who drove the actors at five in the morning, the one who remembered everybody's lines. Somebody decided they belonged on the screen too. Chapter nine of the Lotus Sutra is that part of the credits. Promises of future awakening have been going out to the great disciples, one after another, chapter after chapter. Two people close to the Buddha have been standing nearby the whole time: the man who walked beside him every day, and the boy who was his son. Today: Ananda and Rahula.
screen: `THE NAMES AT THE END OF THE CREDITS.` → `PROMISES GOING OUT.` → `TWO WHO STOOD CLOSEST.`

segments.voice: First, they ask. Ananda and Rahula think, what about us? So they get up, bow at the Buddha's feet, and say it plainly: we have a claim here too. One of us attends you and keeps your teaching. The other is your son. Name us, and our wish is fulfilled. Behind them, a whole crowd of monks, some still in training and some finished, stand up too. Second, the Buddha answers Ananda, and he tells a story with it. Long ago, under a Buddha of a past age, he and Ananda set their minds on awakening together. Ananda gave himself to hearing much. The Buddha gave himself to effort. So one woke first, and the other became the keeper of everything he heard. Neither road is left out. Ananda will be a Buddha too, and hearing the story, he remembers his own old vow. Third, Rahula. The Buddha says Rahula will be the eldest son of future Buddhas, as he is his son now. Then comes a tender line, in paraphrase: Rahula's quiet practice, nobody knows it but me. The one always introduced as somebody's son has a practice of his own, and his father has been watching it. Fourth, why it matters. Being close to someone great can feel like living in their shadow: the assistant, the sibling, the spouse, the kid of the famous one. People thank them in passing, if at all. Chapter nine stops and gives each of them a future, with their own name and their own story. Then it turns to the crowd still standing behind them, and gives them promises too.
screen: `THEY STAND UP AND ASK.` · `ANANDA CHOSE TO HEAR MUCH.` · `RAHULA'S QUIET PRACTICE.` · `NOBODY IS TOO CLOSE TO COUNT.` · then, large: `THEM TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor someone close to a great person. Settle, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind someone whose work makes another person's work possible. The nurse beside the surgeon. The parent who drove a gifted kid to every practice. The sibling of the one everybody talks about. The person who keeps the books at the place you love. See them clearly, their face, their hands, what they carry that nobody claps for. Hold them there for a few breaths. Silently say their name, and one thing they do that nobody thanks them for. Then let them go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ananda and Rahula. The attendant who kept the teaching, and the son with a quiet practice, both given their own promise. Today's word.
Your line: them too. Today, thank one person who works beside someone better known, and use their name when you do. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember Ananda as the attendant who heard and kept the Buddha's teaching, and Rahula as his son who became a monk; in the Lotus Sutra both receive the promise of future buddhahood in chapter nine.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. promises have gone out to the great disciples, one after another. you've walked beside the Buddha every day. what do you do?
options: wait quietly; maybe he'll get to you.
stand up with Rahula, bow, and ask.

fork.reveal: Ananda and Rahula stand up, bow at his feet and ask, saying they have a claim too. the Buddha answers each of them by name.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: joy, delight. the name of the Buddha's attendant.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ananda and Rahula were bystanders while the famous disciples got the promises.
what it means: they stand up, ask for their own promise, and each gets one, with a story of why.
what a scholar hears: the chapter sets Ananda's hearing much beside the Buddha's effort, and treats both as roads to the same awakening.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 9, not quoted (wording unverified). Check: Ananda and Rahula rise, bow and claim a prediction as attendant/keeper of the Law and son; learners and adepts rise with them.
Check the backstory: Ananda and Shakyamuni conceived the aspiration together under a past Buddha; Ananda devoted himself to great learning (bahusruta), Shakyamuni to exertion; Ananda recalls his vow.
Check Rahula's prediction (eldest son of future Buddhas) and the verse about Rahula's hidden/secret practice known only to the Buddha; paraphrased as 'quiet practice'.
Ananda's and Rahula's future Buddha names deliberately left out.
Original: आनन्द (Ānanda), 'joy'; standard lexicon sense, confirm.

Editor: practice now ends by naming the person and one unthanked task, instead of 'wish them well' (day 1159's practice); 'The chapter doesn't treat that as a lesser road' softened to what the text shows.
